name: Face Replacement and Digital Doubles
title: Face Replacement and Digital Doubles
answer: Face replacement and digital doubles cover techniques for swapping one person's face onto another performer's body, creating a synthetic likeness of an actor for stunts, de-aging, or posthumous appearances, and generating fully synthetic human faces for background or principal roles. In cinematography and video synthesis, this spans set extensions, crowd replication, and performance transfer where an actor's facial motion drives a different or synthetic face. The work sits between visual effects, identity preservation, and generative video.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on high-end GPU workstations and render farms, often integrated into compositing and editorial pipelines. Training and inference for face replacement models require substantial video memory and fast storage for high-resolution frame sequences. Many productions use a mix of on-premises systems for security and cloud burst capacity for large batch renders. Real-time previews may run on local workstations with lower fidelity, while final frames are processed offline.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The typical workflow begins with capturing reference footage or a 3D scan of the target face under varied lighting and expression. A model is then trained or fine-tuned to map the source performance onto the target face, often using an autoencoder or diffusion-based architecture with facial landmark alignment and segmentation masks. Artists refine the output with traditional compositing, rotoscoping, and color matching to handle occlusions, motion blur, and hair interaction. Quality control compares the result against reference photography and checks for temporal stability across frames.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on consent, contract terms, and publicity rights. A production should obtain explicit written permission from the actor whose face is replaced or recreated, and from the estate or rights holder for a deceased performer. Union agreements and local laws may limit how a digital double is used, especially for scenes the actor did not perform. Provenance records should document the source footage, model version, artist approvals, and any synthetic elements for audit and chain of title. This page describes practice, not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward real-time face replacement for virtual production and live performance, with lower latency and higher fidelity on set. Generative video models are making it easier to create a digital double from a small set of stills, but temporal consistency and identity preservation remain active problems. Expect tighter integration with performance capture and neural rendering, along with more standardized consent and provenance tooling as productions face scrutiny over synthetic performers.
